opus-5.5.text:
I think data quality is one of the most underappreciated levers we have, and it changes the capacity question quite profoundly. A lot of our work started from looking at what happens when you compress or prune a model. You can remove a huge fraction of the weights, sometimes ninety percent, and top-line accuracy barely moves. So the natural question is: what was all that extra capacity doing?

What we found is that it's disproportionately spent on a relatively small subset of the data, the long tail. These are atypical examples, rare subgroups, and often noisy or mislabeled examples. When you prune, the model forgets those first. The easy, prototypical examples that make up most of the distribution are learned early and cheaply. It's the hard tail that requires the extra capacity, and some of that tail is genuinely valuable rare signal while some of it is just noise the model is memorizing.

So if you improve data quality, if you clean out the mislabeled and corrupted examples or deduplicate redundant ones, you can often get away with a much smaller model, because you're not forcing it to spend parameters memorizing garbage. There's a growing body of work showing that carefully curated, smaller datasets can match or beat much larger ones, and the models trained on them can be more compact.

But there's an important caveat. You have to be careful about how you define "low quality." Many of the examples that look like outliers are actually underrepresented but legitimate cases, say a rare medical condition or a demographic group that's sparse in the training set. If your quality filter treats everything atypical as noise, you'll shrink the model nicely and quietly hurt performance on exactly the groups you most need to get right. That's a fairness issue, not just an efficiency one.

So my view is that data and capacity are deeply coupled. Much of the scaling we've seen has been compensating for messy data with brute-force parameters. If we invest more in understanding our data, separating noise from valuable rare signal, we can build models that are more efficient and also more reliable on the long tail.

r001.rationale: It says carefully curated, smaller datasets can match or outperform larger ones, linking better data quality with needing less training data for comparable performance.

r002.rationale: It explains that models use extra parameters to memorize noisy data and says brute-force capacity compensates for messy data.

r003.rationale: It describes pruning away sometimes 90% of the weights and says pruning makes the model forget long-tail examples, including noisy or mislabeled ones.

r004.rationale: It describes pruning away sometimes 90% of the weights and says pruning makes the model forget long-tail examples, including rare subgroups.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. So I think this is one of the most underappreciated levers we have, and it ties directly into a lot of the work I've been doing on what I'd call the long tail of data.

The way I'd frame it is that there's a very strong, almost orthogonal relationship between how clean or well-curated your data is and how much capacity you need to actually fit it. When we train on a large, noisy corpus, a lot of the parameters in the model are essentially being spent on memorizing or accommodating examples that are either mislabeled, atypical, or just very rare. Our work on compression, pruning and quantization showed this really clearly. When you remove capacity from a model, what gets lost first isn't the average, well-represented example. It's the long tail. The model's performance on the "easy," prototypical examples is remarkably robust to losing a huge fraction of its weights. What degrades is performance on the rare, hard, or noisy examples, which is also where a lot of the fairness and robustness concerns live.

So if you flip that around, the implication is that a big chunk of model capacity is in some sense a tax we pay for messy data. If you clean the data, deduplicate it, correct labels, remove the examples that are actively contradictory, you often find that a smaller model gets you the same or better performance, because it no longer has to dedicate capacity to resolving noise. We saw versions of this at Cohere and in the broader community: careful data curation and filtering can be worth more than scaling parameters, and it compounds with scale rather than being a substitute for it.

That said, I'd push back on the idea that you simply want to make the data as "clean" as possible. Some of what looks like noise is actually signal about the real distribution. Rare examples, underrepresented groups, unusual phrasings, these are exactly the things we want the model to be good at, and if you filter them aggressively you end up with a model that's efficient but brittle, and brittle in ways that disproportionately affect people who are already underrepresented. So I don't think about it as noisy versus clean. I think about it as understanding which examples are expensive for the model to learn and why. Is it expensive because the label is wrong, in which case fix it or drop it? Or is it expensive because it's genuinely rare but important, in which case you probably need to keep it and maybe even upweight it?

The other thing I'd say is that this reframes the whole scaling conversation. We've spent a decade treating parameters and compute as the primary axis, and data quality as this secondary, almost janitorial concern. I think that's backwards. Data is the thing that determines what the model is even trying to learn, and capacity is just how much slack you have to learn it. If we were more systematic about measuring example difficulty and data quality, I think we'd find we could train considerably smaller models, which matters enormously for who gets to participate in this field and for the environmental and economic cost of these systems.

r001.rationale: The response says better curation can let a smaller model achieve similar or better performance, but does not say it reduces the amount of training data needed.

r002.rationale: It explains that model capacity is spent memorizing or accommodating noisy examples, framing some capacity as a tax for messy data.

r003.rationale: It says removing a huge fraction of weights degrades performance on noisy examples, but does not report that removing 90% of parameters causes this.

r004.rationale: It says rare examples are among those lost when capacity is reduced, but does not specify removing 90% of parameters.

astra-6.text:
I think model capacity and data quality are very closely linked. We often talk about the size of a model as if it’s determined just by how difficult the task is, but it also depends on how that task is represented in the data. If you have noisy labels or lots of irrelevant variation, some of the model’s capacity can go toward fitting that noise. With cleaner, more informative data, you may be able to get the same performance with a smaller model.

The caveat is that “cleaner” shouldn’t mean removing everything that’s difficult or unusual. A rare example may look like an outlier, but it could represent something we really need the model to learn. So the question is: are we removing noise, or are we removing meaningful diversity? Those have very different implications for the capacity you need and for who the model works well for.

r001.rationale: It says cleaner data may let the model achieve the same performance with a smaller model, but does not suggest that higher-quality data reduces the amount of training data needed.

r002.rationale: It explains that noisy labels or irrelevant variation consume model capacity, conveying that extra capacity may be spent fitting noisy training data.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss removing 90% of a model’s parameters or forgetting noisy examples.

r004.rationale: It warns that rare examples may be meaningful, but does not report that removing 90% of parameters causes the model to forget rare examples.

sol-6.1.text:
I think data quality and model capacity are deeply intertwined. If your data contains a lot of noise, you may need more capacity simply to fit that noise. So a larger model can compensate for some problems in the data, but that doesn’t necessarily mean it’s learning a better representation of the task.

With cleaner, more informative data, you can often achieve the same performance with a smaller model. But I’d be careful about equating quality with removing everything that’s difficult or unusual. A rare example might look like noise when it actually represents an important part of the population. If you remove those examples, you might make the task easier while making the model less useful.

So the question is really: capacity to learn what? Fitting the training set, generalizing to typical examples, and performing well on underrepresented cases can place very different demands on a model.

r001.rationale: The response says cleaner data may allow a smaller model at the same performance, but does not say higher-quality data could reduce the amount of training data needed.

r002.rationale: It explains that noisy data may require more capacity to fit the noise and that a larger model can compensate for some data problems.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention removing 90% of a model’s parameters or forgetting noisy training examples.

r004.rationale: The response discusses rare examples but does not report that removing 90% of parameters causes a model to forget them.
